I am writing this feedback to express serious concerns regarding the conditions at NSPIRE of Kendall. This facility is extremely dirty, outdated, and poorly maintained. For years, the floors were covered with carpets saturated with patient urine, saliva, and other bodily fluids. Only recently were those carpets removed and replaced with flooring, which should have been done long ago. The beds are old and malfunction frequently. My aunt’s bed barely goes up, making it extremely difficult for the nursing assistants to care for her. It is evident that this puts physical strain on the staff, and I can only imagine the back pain they must endure due to faulty equipment. Additionally, when my aunt was receiving IV antibiotics, she was provided with a severely rusted IV pole base, which is both unsafe and unacceptable. The handrails throughout the facility are visibly filthy, covered in dirt and residue, and on some occasions even contained coffee cups left inside them. When I opened one of the bedside drawers, three cockroaches came out. During all the days my aunt has been at this facility, I have never witnessed any fumigation or pest control services. This facility is in dire need of extensive repairs, proper sanitation, and accountability. I have attempted to report these concerns to the administration on three separate occasions. Each time, the administrative office was closed—morning, afternoon, and evening—making it impossible to file a complaint or receive any response. The conditions at NSPIRE of Kendall are unacceptable for patients, families, and staff. This facility requires immediate attention, repairs, and leadership oversight to ensure a safe and dignified environment for everyone involved.

Review:
My father was admitted to Nspire Healthcare on Friday, July 18, for rehabilitation after surgery. I was present within five minutes of his arrival and made sure to introduce myself to all staff. I let them know we would be checking on him daily—through visits and calls—to ensure he received proper care.

I was told physical therapy (PT) would evaluate him on Saturday, July 19, but no one came. Instead, I learned from his roommate that my father had fallen during the night, and it was the roommate who called for help. Staff never informed me until the following day, and only then did they place fall mats around his bed “just in case.”

Each day, my brother and I made our presence known, checking in and following up. On July 21, PT stood him up briefly on the mat but said he could not stand more than five seconds—even though he had been walking with assistance in the hospital. On July 22, a PT therapist told me my father was “combative” and “did not follow directions.” I reminded them that he has dementia, which should have been clearly noted in his records. The therapist seemed annoyed.

On July 24, after missing a visit the day before due to weather, I found my father in a new room. He was lying in bed with a blank expression, unshaven, wearing a hospital gown despite having four clean changes of clothes I had provided. His sheets were dirty. The TV was on with no volume, and the room felt neglected. When I checked his diaper, it was so soaked with urine it had leaked through the pad and into the bed. I was heartbroken. I cleaned him myself and dressed him.

While packing up his belongings to take him home, staff couldn’t find his shoes. Eventually, they were located in his old room—further proving that no PT had actually been done, since he hadn’t even had his shoes with him in the new room.

I immediately went to the main office and informed Khisha that I was taking my father home. There was no real sense of urgency or concern from the staff. The main nurse seemed unfazed. As I wheeled my father out, Sheldon stopped me and apologized, but by then, the damage was done.

The next day, with the help of his caregiver, I gave my father a proper shower. He screamed in pain from a severe diaper rash that was bleeding. Within two days of being home, he was walking again—like he had been before his surgery.

I truly believe that if I had left my father in that facility, he might not be alive today. What happened was not just neglect—it was a complete failure in basic human care.

If I could give Nspire zero stars, I would. Do NOT bring your loved ones here.

My father is a resident at Nspire, and what I’ve witnessed is absolutely heartbreaking and unacceptable. He has fallen multiple times and was left lying on the floor—naked and alone. Not only is this undignified, but it’s also dangerous.

He cannot feed himself, yet staff routinely drop off his food and walk away. The meals sit untouched and grow cold because no one assists him. On one visit, I was there for over six hours—not once did anyone come to change him or check on him.

The nurses? Sitting at the desk. The aides? Overwhelmed or indifferent. When food was delivered during my visit, the aide casually said, “You can feed him.” When I asked who would feed him if I wasn't there, she responded that she had other residents to tend to. Unacceptable.

The room smelled horribly of neglect, and when concerns are raised, the excuses pile on: “Our backs hurt,” or worse—suggestions that we hire a private nurse on top of the Medicare, Medicaid, and Social Security funds they are already receiving for his care.

This is not just poor service—this is neglect. Nspire is failing its most vulnerable residents while collecting substantial payments. It’s time for lawyers, advocates, and health care authorities to take a hard look at what’s really happening behind these doors.

Our seniors deserve better. My dad deserves better. Enough is enough.

Review: This is review is only for their rehab wing.  Shortly after admission their management team had a meeting with me to discuss my mother's treatment/care strategies.  At the meeting they mentioned 2 accommodations that they would make so that she wouldn't fall off the bed (beds didn't have siderails).  After a few days went by and I didn't see the barriers they mentioned I asked management.  It turns out that the accommodations they mentioned were waiting to be delivered and they had to resort to simply lowering my moms bed every night.  My moms stay ended and those barriers never were installed.  At the same meeting they gave me a treatment plan that was blank and asked me to sign it (before it was completed).  I thought that was a very unprofessional request from their management.  I told them to complete it first, then I would sign it.  Very few CNAs understand English well, but their patient care was professional.  All the nurses and some of the CNAs that worked with my mom seemed bothered when they were called for pain meds (by my mom or her roommate) or anything else for that matter.  The food was consistently delivered timely, well-presented, temperature appropriate, and tasted pretty good.  It takes hours for the meal trays to be removed though.  Sometimes my mom would have 2 meal trays in her room at the same time, I would be the one to move the unused one to the hallway.  Even when moved to the hallway they would sit there for hours.  Linens:  I saw blankets with holes the size of dinner plates in them in use.  I am not exaggerating.  The CNAs would do their best to fold them in a way that they weren't easily visible but too late, I saw it, each time.  Resident rooms and bathrooms were kept clean.  Every interaction with a social worker or PT staff member was professional and helpful.  The hallways and nursing station was a literal mess and not neat at all.  Hallways were cluttered with unused furniture, office fixtures, and all sorts of other equipment and supplies.  The carpeted areas were filthy.  Also, I found it odd that none of their nurses/CNAs wore name tags.  Personally, due to the interactions I had (and witnessed my mom's roommate have) with the nurses and CNAs, I would never willingly put a family member there again unless there is no other available option.
